Equal Angles In Crossed Circles

GeometryCircles
Game: Two circles overlap and a straight line cuts across both; watch two pairs of angles that stay equal as the circles change.
How to play: Drag the four dots S, T, RB and RS with a mouse or finger, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Press Statement or Extra to show the marked angles and the dashed lines.
Look for the math

Two circles cross at S and T. A straight chord of one cuts the other at P and Q. The page claims that the angle at S marked by A and P equals the angle at T marked by B and Q — and that a second pair, B,S,Q and A,T,P, is equal too. The live cut-the-knot page still embeds Bogomolny's Java applet; this page draws the same construction with draggable points. It is a picture to explore, not a game to win.

Two four-corner circles

ASTB is a four-corner circle: all four points lie on the larger circle, so its opposite angles add to 180°. PSTQ lies on the smaller one, so its opposite angles do the same. Using the outside-angle relation at S and then at Q:

∠ASP = ∠AST − ∠PST
     = (180° − ∠ABT) − (180° − ∠PQT)
     = ∠BTQ.

Because A, P, Q and B are on one straight line, the two angles being subtracted are the angles that line makes at B and at Q; their difference is exactly the angle at T between TB and TQ.

The second pair

Angles standing on the same arc are equal: ∠ASB = ∠ATB in the larger circle and ∠PSQ = ∠PTQ in the smaller. Subtracting twice equal angles from equal angles leaves ∠ATP = ∠BSQ. Press Extra to see the dashed lines SB, SQ, TA and TP that frame this second pair.

What the checks found

The logic test compares the page with a second transcription of the applet's bytecode on the opening picture, sweeps of every handle and over 3,000 random configurations. On every non-degenerate drawing where the chord of one circle really crosses the other (the picture the page describes), both angle pairs agree to better than a billionth of a radian, and the two four-corner relations hold. The claim is not unconditional: drag the chord clear of the shared lens, so P and Q lie outside the span AB, and the marked angles need not match; the test pins down such a counterexample. If S or T lands on the chord the picture collapses and there are no arcs to compare, so the test leaves those cases out. Two faithful quirks remain: the applet calls the left point S regardless of which handle was dragged there, it calls the larger-radius circle the big one, and when S and T come within one unit it keeps the previous picture. This is different from the sibling applet Equal Angles In Crossing Circles, which claims equal chord lengths AB = CD for two lines through a crossing point and has switches for adjusting circles or chords; here there is one chord and no lengths to compare.

Turn on Statement and Extra, then drag RS until P and Q slide between A and B: the two readouts stay equal. Now pull the chord outside the shared lens and watch them part company.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
